description: Soy Fátima, estudiante de Ingeniería Mecatrónica con experiencia en CAD, Arduino/ESP32 y PLC. He llevado ideas de la mesa de diseño a prototipos reales (cosechadora de yuca, dron de vigilancia). Me apasiona el espacio y el ambiente: participé en la Olimpiada de Astronomía y fui voluntaria en reforestación. Aportaré hardware y una interfaz física multisensorial. Busco: desarrollador/a de software, perfil de audio/sonificación, UX/UI y experto/a en datos de la NASA. ¡Únete!
summary:
Project Tropical Data turns NASA ocean data into sound. Our web app, Earth Jukebox: Listening Lab, lets anyone pick an ocean location (such as the Niño 3.4 region, the Gulf of Mexico or the Western Pacific warm pool), press Play and hear sea-surface conditions change month by month while NASA's Scientific Visualization Studio animation (SVS 5101, an Earth Information Center visualization) steps through time. Warmer values produce a higher pitch, a glide shows the direction of change, and the number of pulses shows how big the change is.

We answer the Earth Information Jukebox challenge by making climate data something you can hear, not only see. This matters for people who are blind or have low vision, and for anyone who understands patterns better by ear. Every sound has a written equivalent, every control works with a keyboard or mouse, and every number links back to its NASA source. We also built a physical controller with an ESP32 and two joysticks, so visitors in a museum or classroom can explore the data hands-on.

Our data pipeline supports NASA's measured MUR sea-surface temperature. The current demo sonifies the colours of the NASA visualization and labels this clearly on screen.
details:
What it does and how it works

Earth Jukebox: Listening Lab is a web app that turns NASA sea-surface data into sound. The user picks one of five ocean locations (Western Pacific warm pool, Central equatorial Pacific / Niño 3.4, Gulf of Mexico, North Atlantic and Southern Ocean) and presses Play. The app then steps through 12 monthly observations (Nov 2025 – Oct 2026) of NASA Scientific Visualization Studio animation 5101, which is tagged "Earth Information Center" and is built from the MUR v4.1 sea-surface temperature product.

Each observation becomes a short sound:

- Pitch = value. Warmer water gives a higher tone (220–880 Hz).

- Glide = direction. A rising or falling glide shows whether the value went up or down since the previous month.

- Pulses = size of change. One to five pulses show how big the change was.

- Voice = place. Each region has its own instrument, so listeners can tell locations apart by ear.

The map, the numeric readout, a plain-language "In words" description and the sound all come from a single app state, so what you see, read and hear always matches. Every number links to its NASA source file.

Benefits and expected impact

Climate data is usually shown only as colour maps, which excludes people who are blind or have low vision and can overwhelm general audiences. Our project makes ocean warming patterns audible, so they can be understood without seeing the screen. Every sound has a text equivalent, and every control works by mouse, keyboard or our physical controller. We see it being used in museums, classrooms and science outreach events, where visitors can "listen" to El Niño or compare the tropics with the Southern Ocean.

Physical controller

We built a hands-on controller with an ESP32 board and two analog joysticks. Joystick 1 changes the date (left/right), the location (up/down) and plays/pauses when pressed. Joystick 2 controls volume and mute. The ESP32 sends simple JSON messages over USB, and the browser reads them with the Web Serial API. No drivers or extra software are needed beyond Chrome or Edge.

Tools and technologies

- Web app: React, TypeScript, Vite, MapLibre GL (map) and Tone.js (audio synthesis with a limiter for safe listening levels), with automated tests in Vitest.

- Data pipeline: Python with xarray, NumPy, Pillow, OpenEXR and earthaccess (NASA Earthdata).

- Hardware: ESP32-WROOM-32E (CRCibernética board), two KY-023 joysticks and Arduino IDE (C++).

- Data: NASA SVS 5101 frames and GHRSST MUR v4.1 sea-surface temperature (NASA JPL / PO.DAAC).

What makes it creative

Instead of another chart, we treat the ocean as a musical instrument. Each region "plays" its own climate story, and the joystick turns data exploration into something physical and playful, like a jukebox for the planet.

Factors we considered

- Scientific honesty: the current demo sonifies the colours of NASA's visualization because Earthdata credentials were not available in time. The app labels this clearly ("Visual feature mode – not temperature"), and the pipeline can switch to measured MUR temperatures with one command.

- Accessibility: keyboard navigation, text equivalents for every sound, and no information carried by colour alone.

- Hearing safety: an audio limiter, a volume control, mute, and audio that only starts after the user presses Play.

- Robustness: invalid or missing data produces silence plus a written message instead of a misleading sound, and the app keeps working if the controller is unplugged.
